name: Revigator

card.summary: A 1910s-1930s ceramic crock lined with radioactive ore that was sold to infuse drinking water with radon for general vitality and health.
card.aka: radium water jar, Radium Ore Revigator
card.note: Historical device; stored water was later measured to contain radon and toxic metals including arsenic and lead.

quick.overview:
The Revigator was a water crock whose liner contained radioactive ore. Users filled it overnight and drank the water through the day. In the 1920s and 1930s it was marketed as a way to feel more vigorous and healthy, part of a wider radium health fad.

In a looks context it belongs to the history of wellness products sold for vitality and general health. Advertisers claimed benefits such as relief from arthritis and senility, rather than specific cosmetic effects.
quick.how: Marketing instructions told users to fill the jar each night and drink freely, six or more glasses a day [1]. It is now a collectors' and history item, not something sold for use.
quick.risks: A modern analysis of water stored in a vintage unit found high radon, plus arsenic, lead, vanadium and uranium at levels posing health risks [1][2].

lead: The Revigator was a ceramic water crock lined with carnotite ore containing uranium and radium. Patented in 1912 by R. W. Thomas, it was sold by Dow-Herriman Pump & Machinery Company after 1924 and moved thousands of units in the 1920s and 1930s [1].
Users filled it overnight so the water would take up radiation, then drank it the next day. Advertising claimed it could help with arthritis, flatulence and senility [1].
A 2009 analytical study titled 'What were they drinking?' examined water from a vintage Revigator with spectroscopic and radiation methods [2].

angle.text: The device was sold as a daily health tonic, and its appearance relevance is a claimed general vitality benefit typical of the radium-tonic era.

paras: Thomas patented the design in 1912 while working as a stock salesman in Arizona, moved to southern California by 1923 to manufacture it, and sold the operation in 1924 to Dow-Herriman, which sold thousands [1]. Several successful ad campaigns created demand he could not meet [1].

Analysis of water stored in a vintage unit found high radon along with arsenic, lead from the spout, vanadium and uranium at levels posing health risks. A study at Mount St. Mary's University concluded that the radiation risk was probably low compared with other causes of death of the time [1][2].
No studies found. Only an analytical chemistry study of the device's water exists [2].

timeline.event: R. W. Thomas patents the device [1]
